summary: Shock is tissue hypoperfusion, not hypotension. Identify the broken part fast — tank (hypovolemic), pump (cardiogenic), blocked flow (obstructive), or wide pipes (distributive) — then fix it specifically. The first three are low-CO / high-SVR states; distributive is the low-SVR state.

body.text: Shock = acute circulatory failure where oxygen delivery is insufficient for cellular metabolic demand. Hypotension is common but not required; tissue hypoperfusion is the defining event.
The four types

rows: Low preload drops CO; compensatory vasoconstriction
CI ≤ 2.2; backup pressure into the lungs
Mechanical barrier to filling or outflow
Pathologic vasodilation; high CO early, can drop later

body.text: Distributive shock usually runs a high CO early; sepsis-related myocardial depression can drop CO later (~40% of septic shock has demonstrable cardiac dysfunction). The first three types are low-CO states; distributive is the low-SVR state.
Hypovolemic — the tank is empty

Signature: CO ↓, CVP ↓, PCWP ↓, SVR ↑, HR ↑. Hemorrhagic (trauma, GI bleed, ruptured AAA, postpartum hemorrhage — ATLS Class I–IV, up to 40% volume loss before frank hypotension) or non-hemorrhagic (DKA, vomiting/diarrhea, burns, third-spacing, pancreatitis, bowel obstruction) — same hemodynamic picture, no blood loss. Echo: small hyperdynamic LV, kissing walls at end-systole, flat IVC (< 2 cm, > 50% collapse). Treat with volume (blood if hemorrhagic, crystalloid if not), fix the source; permissive hypotension in uncontrolled hemorrhage until surgical control.
Cardiogenic — the pump is failing

Signature: CI ≤ 2.2, PCWP > 15–18, SVR ↑, CVP ↑. LV failure (AMI — especially anterior STEMI — decompensated HF, myocarditis, takotsubo): cold extremities, pulmonary edema, elevated JVP, S3. RV failure (RV infarct, massive PE, pulmonary HTN crisis): elevated JVP, clear lungs, worse with nitrates or diuresis. Mechanical (acute MR from papillary muscle rupture, acute VSD, free-wall rupture): a new murmur + collapse is a surgical emergency. Arrhythmic (VT/VF, complete heart block, very rapid SVT): fix the rhythm first.
SCAI SHOCK stages (A → E)

rows: No signs/symptoms of CS but at risk (large AMI, prior HF). Normal hemodynamics, lactate ≤ 2, warm, clear mentation.
Relative hypotension or tachycardia without hypoperfusion. Filling pressures may be up. Critical window — highest progression risk within 24 h.
Hypoperfusion requiring pharmacologic or mechanical support. Lactate > 2. Cold extremities, altered mentation, rising creatinine.
Failure of initial support — requires TIME spent in Stage C first. Rising lactate and/or escalating vasopressor / MCS need.
Lactate > 8. Profound hypotension despite maximal support. Actual or impending collapse, arrest in progress.

body.text: The cardiac-arrest modifier (subscript A, e.g. C-A, E-A) means arrest with coma — worse outcome at ANY stage. A common error is assuming every post-arrest patient is automatically Stage E; conflating prior arrest with refractory shock hides reversible cardiogenic shock behind irreversible anoxic injury. Stage D requires time spent failing an adequate trial of support, not just worse numbers at one moment; a catastrophic event can jump a patient straight to E. Most stage changes happen in the first 24 h — reassess constantly.
Obstructive — something is blocking flow
Signature: CO ↓, CVP ↑, PCWP variable. Vasopressors are a bridge; definitive treatment removes the obstruction.

rows: Pericardial fluid compresses chambers → impaired diastolic filling. Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled sounds, JVD), pulsus paradoxus > 10 mmHg. Treat: pericardiocentesis.

Mediastinal shift impairs venous return. Absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation, distended neck veins. Clinical diagnosis — decompress immediately (needle 2nd ICS MCL or 4th/5th ICS AAL), then chest tube.
Clot burden → RV outflow obstruction and acute RV failure. RV dilation, D-sign, McConnell's sign. Clot-directed treatment: thrombolysis, catheter-directed therapy, or surgical embolectomy.

body.text: Distributive — the pipes are too wide
Signature: CO usually ↑, SVR ↓, CVP ↓ early, PCWP variable.

rows: Dysregulated host response → massive vasodilation, capillary leak. Sepsis-3: suspected infection + SOFA ≥ 2; septic shock = vasopressor-dependent MAP ≥ 65 + lactate > 2. Early: warm, flushed, bounding. Late: can turn cold; ~40% have cardiac dysfunction.
IgE-mediated histamine release → vasodilation + bronchospasm. IM epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg (1:1000) is the first and only essential treatment; antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts.
SCI above T6 → loss of sympathetic tone. Triad: hypotension + bradycardia + warm skin. Norepinephrine or phenylephrine; atropine for symptomatic bradycardia.
Post-bypass vasoplegia, adrenal crisis, pancreatitis, capillary leak syndrome, myxedema coma.

body.text: The 60-second bedside algorithm

items: Touch the patient. Warm → distributive. Cold → cardiogenic, hypovolemic, or obstructive.
Look at the neck veins. Flat → hypovolemic or early distributive. Distended → cardiogenic, obstructive, or late distributive.
Listen to the lungs. Wet (B-lines/crackles) → cardiogenic LV failure. Clear + JVD → RV failure, tamponade, PE, or neurogenic.
Grab the ultrasound. LV function? RV dilation? Pericardial effusion? IVC size and collapsibility? Free fluid?
Ask: is this mixed? If the hemodynamics don't fit one box, or the patient isn't responding, it's probably more than one box.

rows: Small LV, flat/collapsing IVC, kissing walls
Depressed LV/RV, wall-motion abnormalities, dilated IVC, B-lines
RA/RV diastolic collapse, IVC plethora, swinging heart

Mixed shock — the rule, not the exception, in sick patients
Mixed shock is the second most common shock type in contemporary cardiac ICUs. When hemodynamics don't fit one box, get the echo and consider a PA catheter.

rows: Distributive + cardiogenic. ~40% of septic shock has cardiac dysfunction; the initial high CO can mask it.
Cardiogenic + distributive — the 'warm and wet' CS phenotype: SIRS from myocardial necrosis lowers SVR despite LV failure.
Hypovolemic + obstructive — two independent mechanisms stacking, each needing its own treatment.
Primary mixed: myocardial stunning (cardiogenic) + vasoplegia (distributive). Needs both vasopressors and inotropes.

body.text: Cardiogenic-vasodilatory shock = cardiogenic + inappropriate vasodilation; vasodilatory-cardiogenic = vasodilatory + myocardial dysfunction; primary mixed shock has simultaneous onset (post-arrest). Both CO and SVR have to be addressed regardless of which label fits best. Shock is physiology, not a diagnosis — identify the broken part, fix it specifically, reassess constantly.
2026 note — penetrating tamponade without thoracotomy

A 2026 single-center case series (25 consecutive patients, penetrating cardiac tamponade, resource-limited high-volume trauma center) used ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis via a 16G dialysis catheter + 1 g intrapericardial tranexamic acid + a pericardial drain for 48 h with serial echo: 96% survival to discharge (24/25), thoracotomy avoided in 100%, 8% recurrence (2 patients, managed without thoracotomy). Rationale for intrapericardial TXA: pericardial blood is a strong local fibrinolytic stimulus, and instilled TXA is theorized to stabilize clot at the source after drainage without the systemic bleeding tradeoff of IV dosing. Caveat: an extreme-environment case series — it does not replace thoracotomy where surgical capability exists; it documents what is possible when it does not.
